attribution.note: Marcus wrote this sentence in his own Substack post. It is his own claim, not a quotation.

semantics.note: The wording is firm and unhedged ('has made'). It claims that scaling caused a gain in authority but no gain in truthfulness. The normalised version keeps both parts. Calling it causal is reasonable.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: the claim is limited to language models and judged by same-family size comparisons up to February 2023. The result depends on choices Marcus never made: which model families count, whether generated or multiple-choice answers count, and how to measure authority.

evidence.note: TruthfulQA (2021), a primary source dated before the post, found that the largest models were generally the least truthful when generating answers. This covers the GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2 and T5 families. It supports the 'not more truthful' part for these families only.

In the Gopher paper, published before the post, TruthfulQA multiple-choice accuracy rose with size within the Gopher family across several test setups. This is a comparable test showing truthfulness gains, though it measures picking answers, not writing them.

reviews.rationale: The 'not more truthful' part holds for the families tested in TruthfulQA (e1), where bigger models were less truthful in generated answers. Gopher's same-family multiple-choice results (e2) show truthfulness improving with size, so the general claim fails. The 'more authoritative-sounding' part was not measured in any evidence item and stays unsettled. The contract says that pattern counts as mixed.
